chapter_title: The History and Evolution of Programmable Logic
chapter_summary:
The story of programmable logic begins in the 1970s with **Programmable Read-Only Memory (PROM)** devices. A PROM is a memory chip that can be programmed once with a fixed truth table. Engineers realized that a PROM could be used as a lookup table to implement any combinational logic function. By storing the output of a Boolean function for every possible input combination, a PROM could replace a network of gates. However, PROMs were inefficient because they required 2^n memory locations for n inputs, making them impractical for functions with more than a few inputs.

In the late 1970s, **Monolithic Memories Inc. (MMI)** introduced the **Programmable Array Logic (PAL)** device. A PAL combined a programmable AND array with a fixed OR array, making it much more efficient than a PROM for logic implementation. PALs could implement multiple Boolean functions with shared product terms. The PAL architecture was revolutionary because it allowed engineers to replace dozens of discrete logic chips with a single programmable device. MMI's PAL Handbook became the bible of digital design for a generation.

In the 1980s, **Altera** (founded in 1983) introduced the **Erasable Programmable Logic Device (EPLD)** and later the **CPLD**. Altera's MAX series used an EEPROM-based programmable interconnect, allowing devices to be erased and reprogrammed electrically. CPLDs became the standard for simple glue logic and state machines.

The true revolution came in 1985 when **Ross Freeman**, an engineer at **Xilinx**, invented the **Field Programmable Gate Array**. Freeman's insight was to create a device with a two-dimensional array of small logic blocks, each connected to its neighbors through a programmable routing network. The first Xilinx FPGA, the XC2064, had 64 configurable logic blocks (CLBs) and was manufactured on a 2.5-micron process. Today, a single Xilinx Versal FPGA contains billions of transistors and hundreds of thousands of CLBs.

The FPGA industry has evolved through several generations:
- **First Generation (1985–1995):** Simple LUT-based logic, limited routing, used for prototyping and glue logic.
- **Second Generation (1995–2005):** Embedded block RAM, multipliers, and Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs) for clock generation. FPGAs became viable for signal processing.
- **Third Generation (2005–2015):** Embedded hard processors (ARM cores), high-speed transceivers, and PCIe interfaces. FPGAs became System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms.
- **Fourth Generation (2015–present):** AI/ML accelerators, High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools, and advanced packaging (3D stacking). FPGAs compete with GPUs in data centers.

The major FPGA vendors today are:
- **AMD (formerly Xilinx):** The inventor of the FPGA. Current families include Artix-7, Kintex-7, Virtex-7, Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+, and Versal.
- **Intel (formerly Altera):** Acquired by Intel in 2015. Current families include MAX 10, Cyclone V, Arria 10, Stratix 10, and Agilex.
- **Lattice Semiconductor:** Focuses on low-power and small-form-factor FPGAs. Families include iCE40, MachXO, and ECP.
- **Microchip (formerly Microsemi):** Focuses on radiation-tolerant and security-focused FPGAs. Families include IGLOO, ProASIC, and SmartFusion.

A key trend is the integration of **hard intellectual property (IP)** blocks directly into the FPGA silicon. Modern FPGAs contain hard ARM Cortex-A9 or Cortex-A53 processors, DDR memory controllers, PCIe Gen4 interfaces, and even AI/ML inference engines. This transforms the FPGA from a pure logic device into a complete heterogeneous computing platform.

screens.title: The History and Evolution of Programmable Logic
screens.subtitle: How PROMs, PALs, CPLDs, and FPGAs reshaped digital design

narration.text: This chapter tells the engineering story of programmable logic and why it matters for embedded systems today. You will trace a clear line from early PROM lookup tables in the 1970s, to PALs that made gate networks compact, to Altera’s EEPROM-based CPLDs, and finally to Ross Freeman’s 1985 invention of the FPGA. We’ll examine how successive generations added memory, DSP blocks, hard processors, and AI accelerators. I will point out concrete examples you can test: the XC2064, the first Xilinx device with 64 configurable logic blocks, and modern Versal-class chips that integrate billions of transistors and dedicated IP. Along the way we’ll clarify common confusions — for instance, why a CPLD is not simply a smaller FPGA and why PROMs are impractical for many-input functions. By the end you’ll be able to compare devices by capability, explain the design insight behind the FPGA routing fabric, and choose which vendor families to evaluate for low-power or high-throughput applications. Consider this chapter the historical map that makes architectural choices easier to understand. Which era do you think most changed the trajectory of embedded acceleration?

keyIdea.title: Why history matters
keyIdea.text: Understanding the progression from PROM to FPGA explains design trade-offs: density, reprogrammability, and integration of hard IP that enable modern heterogeneous systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will know and be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives guide your learning through the history and engineering choices of programmable logic. First, you will be able to trace the development from PROMs to PALs, to CPLDs, and finally to FPGAs. That means recognizing how each step altered trade-offs in density, reprogrammability, and routing. Second, you will explain Ross Freeman’s 1985 insight that an array of small logic blocks plus a programmable routing fabric made scalable reconfigurability possible, and you will contrast Xilinx’s FPGA birthplace with Altera’s contributions to CPLDs. Third, you will describe the generational technological trends — how embedded memory, DSP multipliers, hard processors, and HLS tooling changed what designers can accomplish on a single chip. Fourth, you will identify the major FPGA vendors and their representative product families so you can pick options for low-power, high-throughput, or security-focused projects. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters in embedded system selection and design. After completing this chapter, you’ll be ready to compare device datasheets with informed expectations rather than guesswork.

screens.title: PROMs: The Lookup-Table Origin
screens.subtitle: How programmable read-only memory implemented logic functions

narration.text: Start with PROMs to ground the lineage. A PROM is a memory chip that can be programmed once with a fixed truth table. Engineers discovered that by storing the outputs for every input combination, a PROM becomes a lookup table that implements any combinational Boolean function. Concretely, if a function has n inputs, the PROM needs 2 to the n memory locations, which grows exponentially and becomes impractical for more than a few inputs. For example, a three‑input function needs eight storage entries; a ten‑input function would need 1,024 entries. This exponential scaling is the core limitation. PROMs were useful for simple glue logic and small replacement of discrete gates, but they were wasteful of silicon for larger logic. A common misconception is to assume a PROM is flexible enough for complex logic; in practice the memory cost and timing overhead make PROMs a poor fit beyond toy examples. Key takeaway: PROMs showed the power of a memory-based mapping from inputs to outputs but also highlighted the need for more efficient architectures that avoid 2^n storage. Reflect: when might a lookup-table approach still be the simplest practical choice?

keyIdea.title: PROM concept
keyIdea.text: PROMs implemented logic via lookup tables but required 2^n storage entries, making them inefficient for many-input functions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › PROMs: The Lookup-Table Origin
Definition

PROM as a logic LUT

A PROM stores a fixed truth table. For every possible input vector it holds the corresponding output word, so the chip acts as a lookup table for combinational logic.

• Storage requirement grows as 2^n for n inputs.
• Efficient for small functions; impractical for wide inputs.
• Timing overhead comes from memory access rather than gate-level evaluation.
Concrete example
A 3-input truth table needs eight entries. A 10-input function needs 1,024 entries, showing the exponential cost quickly becomes prohibitive.
Common mistake
Assuming PROMs scale well. They are simple but expensive in memory and wiring for many inputs.
Analogy

Think of a PROM as a printed reference table: for each input you look up the answer. That simplicity is powerful for small tables but impossible to carry when the table grows huge.

Why it matters
Understanding PROMs clarifies why alternative programmable architectures sought to avoid exponential storage and share product terms across functions.
Check your understanding
Name one situation where a PROM LUT is acceptable and one where it fails due to scaling.

screens.title: PALs: Efficient Programmable Logic
screens.subtitle: How PAL architecture improved on PROM inefficiencies

narration.text: In the late 1970s Monolithic Memories Inc. introduced Programmable Array Logic, or PAL devices, and that was a practical leap. A PAL uses a programmable AND array feeding a fixed OR array. This structure lets designers share product terms among multiple outputs, reducing the amount of storage or logic needed compared to a straight lookup table. The practical result was that a single PAL could replace dozens of discrete gates, making boards simpler and faster to prototype. Engineers treated PALs as the first commercially useful programmable glue logic that scaled beyond tiny PROM examples. A common misconception is to equate PALs with full reconfigurable devices; PALs were targeted, efficient, and limited — they implemented combinational logic well but were not designed for large-scale routing or extensive logic reuse across many blocks. The PAL Handbook became a foundational resource because it showed how to use programmable product terms to express many Boolean functions efficiently. Example: a few shared product terms can implement several state-machine outputs without duplicating gate networks. Takeaway: PALs demonstrate the value of architectural constraints that trade generality for silicon efficiency.

keyIdea.title: PAL advantage
keyIdea.text: PALs reduced resource needs by sharing product terms via a programmable AND array with a fixed OR array, making them efficient for glue logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › PALs: Efficient Programmable Logic
Core Concept

Programmable AND, fixed OR

PALs used a programmable AND array feeding a fixed OR array. Sharing product terms across outputs reduced silicon compared to a full lookup memory.

• Replaced many discrete gates with a single device.
• Efficient for multiple Boolean functions using shared terms.
• Targeted at glue logic and small state machines.
Concrete scenario
A control board with multiple related output signals can compute shared product terms once and feed them to several outputs, saving silicon and wiring complexity.
Historical note

MMI’s PAL architecture and handbook became standard reference material for generations of digital designers because it showed how to structure programmable logic for practical engineering use.

Common misconception
Do not confuse PALs with general reconfigurable arrays. PALs are constrained in architecture to gain efficiency, not breadth of routing or scale.
Key Takeaway

By structuring programmability, PALs offered a practical balance between flexibility and silicon efficiency that PROMs could not match.

screens.title: CPLDs and Altera: Reprogrammability Arrives
screens.subtitle: How CPLDs and EEPROM interconnect changed practical programmability

narration.text: In the 1980s Altera introduced erasable programmable logic devices and later CPLDs that used EEPROM-based interconnect to allow electrical erasure and reprogramming. This was an important practical advance because it let designers update logic without replacing silicon. CPLDs, including Altera’s MAX series, became the go-to option for glue logic and small state machines due to their stability and non-volatility. The CPLD architecture often groups logic into macrocells with a relatively fixed interconnect structure, which yields predictable timing and behavior for control-dominated designs. A key contrast to remember is that CPLDs emphasize deterministic interconnect and non-volatile configuration, while early FPGAs emphasized routing flexibility with volatile configuration memory. Many learners mistakenly treat CPLDs as simply small FPGAs; the difference is in intended use and internal organization. CPLDs remain valuable in designs where stable, non-volatile logic and predictable startup behavior are required. Example: a hardware reset controller or power management sequencer is an ideal CPLD use because the logic must be present and stable immediately at power-up. CPLDs and Altera: Reprogrammability Arrives means cplds provided erasable, reprogrammable logic with eeprom interconnect, excelling at glue logic and deterministic control tasks.. In practical terms, how cplds and eeprom interconnect changed practical programmability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CPLD role
keyIdea.text: CPLDs provided erasable, reprogrammable logic with EEPROM interconnect, excelling at glue logic and deterministic control tasks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › CPLDs and Altera: Reprogrammability Arrives
Process Flow

EEPROM-based reprogrammability

Altera’s CPLDs used erasable programmable interconnects so chips could be updated electrically. This delivered stable, non-volatile configuration useful for control tasks and production hardware.

• Non-volatile configuration avoids external boot memories.
• Predictable startup behavior suits power controllers and sequencers.
• Macrocells and grouped logic simplify timing analysis.
Concrete example
Use a CPLD for a board’s reset and power sequencing so the control logic is present immediately at power-up without external configuration steps.
Comparison
CPLD: non-volatile, deterministic interconnect. Early FPGA: volatile configuration, flexible routing and scalable CLB arrays. Choose CPLD for stable control logic; choose FPGA for flexible, high-density logic and heavy parallelism.
Common mistake
Treating CPLDs as miniature FPGAs. Their architecture and use cases differ: CPLDs prioritize startup stability and simpler interconnects.
Key Takeaway

CPLDs filled the practical niche of non-volatile, reprogrammable glue logic before FPGAs became dense and connected enough to subsume many roles.

screens.title: Xilinx and the FPGA Breakthrough
screens.subtitle: Ross Freeman’s routing-network idea and the XC2064

narration.text: Ross Freeman’s invention of the FPGA in 1985 is the defining moment in programmable logic history. His core idea was to arrange many small logic blocks in a two-dimensional grid and connect them with a programmable routing fabric. This arrangement allowed arbitrary local interconnects and scalable reuse of logic blocks, avoiding the exponential storage cost of PROMs and the limited interconnect of PALs and CPLDs. The first Xilinx device, the XC2064, had 64 configurable logic blocks and was built on a 2.5 micron process. That modest part illustrated the power of routing plus local logic: designers could map varied functions onto the same substrate and reprogram the mapping. A common misconception is that the FPGA was simply a larger PAL. In fact, the routing fabric and uniform logic block model made it a fundamentally different and more general platform. Example: implementing parallel signal-processing pipelines became feasible because each CLB and connection could be placed and routed independently across the array. Takeaway: the FPGA’s architecture separated logic capacity from fixed truth-table size and unlocked scalable parallelism. Xilinx and the FPGA Breakthrough means a grid of small logic blocks plus a programmable routing network made general, scalable reconfigurable hardware possible.. In practical terms, ross freeman’s routing-network idea and the xc2064. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: FPGA insight
keyIdea.text: A grid of small logic blocks plus a programmable routing network made general, scalable reconfigurable hardware possible.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Xilinx and the FPGA Breakthrough
Core Idea

Two-dimensional CLB array + routing

The FPGA decoupled function mapping from fixed tables by offering many small logic blocks and a programmable routing fabric connecting neighbors. This allowed general reconfiguration and parallel placements of logic.

• XC2064 was the first Xilinx FPGA with 64 configurable logic blocks on a 2.5 µm process.
• Routing fabric provides arbitrary local interconnects and scalability.
• Enables design reuse and spatial parallelism for signal processing.
Example
Map a small FIR filter across nearby CLBs to implement a pipeline; the routing fabric connects taps without fixed truth-table growth.
Misconception

Do not view FPGAs as merely larger PALs. The routing concept makes them general spatial computing fabrics, not just bigger programmable gates.

Why engineers care
Routing plus CLBs lets designers trade place-and-route decisions for algorithmic parallelism and reusability across projects.
Check
Explain in one sentence why routing flexibility is more powerful than larger lookup memory.

screens.title: Generational Evolution of FPGAs
screens.subtitle: From LUTs to AI accelerators — four FPGA generations

narration.text: FPGAs evolved in clear generations that reflect added silicon capabilities. First generation devices, roughly 1985–1995, were simple LUT-based logic with limited routing and were used mainly for prototyping and glue logic. The second generation, from about 1995–2005, added embedded block R A M, multipliers, and PLLs, which made FPGAs viable for signal-processing tasks. Third-generation devices, 2005–2015, integrated hard processors such as ARM cores, high-speed transceivers, and PCIe interfaces, effectively turning FPGAs into SoC platforms. The fourth generation, 2015 to present, targets AI/ML acceleration, high-level synthesis tooling, and advanced packaging techniques like 3D stacking. Each generation shifts how engineers use FPGAs: first for logic replacement, then for DSP workloads, later for embedded systems with hard processors, and now for heterogeneous cloud and edge acceleration. A misconception is expecting a single FPGA family to be optimal for all these roles. In reality, vendor families specialize: some prioritize low power and form factor, others prioritize transceivers and throughput, and some aim at AI performance. Consider how Moore’s Law enabled these transitions by increasing transistor budgets and letting designers allocate silicon to hard IP blocks as well as fabric.

keyIdea.title: Generational shifts
keyIdea.text: Each FPGA generation added new class-level capabilities — memory, DSP, hard CPUs, and AI accelerators — changing typical applications and design choices.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Generational Evolution of FPGAs
Timeline
First Gen (1985–1995)
Simple LUT-based logic for prototyping and glue logic.
Second Gen (1995–2005)
Added block RAM, multipliers and PLLs; viable for DSP.
Third Gen (2005–2015)
Embedded hard processors, high-speed transceivers, PCIe — SoC-style FPGAs.
Fourth Gen (2015–present)
AI/ML accelerators, HLS, and advanced packaging for heterogeneous compute.
Why this matters

Knowing the generation helps you choose the right family: DSP-heavy projects favor second-generation features, embedded systems favor third-generation SoC integration, and AI tasks benefit from fourth-generation accelerators and HLS support.

Misconception check
Do not assume newer generation always means better for your use. A low-power IoT node may prefer a small, older-family device optimized for power over a large AI-targeted chip.
Key Takeaway

Match generation attributes to system needs: memory and DSP for signal work, hard CPUs for software-rich systems, and AI features for inference tasks.

screens.title: Vendors and Families
screens.subtitle: Who makes FPGAs today and what they target

narration.text: Understanding vendor families is essential when selecting an FPGA. The major vendors named in this chapter are AMD (formerly Xilinx), Intel (formerly Altera), Lattice Semiconductor, and Microchip (formerly Microsemi). Each vendor and family tends to emphasize different design points. AMD/Xilinx families include Artix-7, Kintex-7, Virtex-7, Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+, and Versal; they span low-cost logic devices to Versal-class heterogeneous platforms. Intel’s portfolio includes MAX 10, Cyclone V, Arria 10, Stratix 10, and Agilex, covering low-power parts to high-performance datacenter targets. Lattice focuses on low-power, small form factors like iCE40, MachXO, and ECP families. Microchip provides radiation-tolerant and security-oriented parts such as IGLOO, ProASIC, and SmartFusion. A common pitfall is assuming feature parity across families: for example, not all families include embedded hard processors or high-speed transceivers. When picking a device, read the datasheet to confirm presence of memory blocks, DSP multipliers, the number of logic cells, and the availability of hard IP like DDR controllers. Example: for a battery-powered sensor node, a Lattice iCE40 or a small Artix variant typically trumps a Versal due to power and cost constraints. The right family balances capability, power, and form factor.

keyIdea.title: Vendor specialization
keyIdea.text: Vendor families differ by power, density, and integrated IP; pick a family based on the application’s power and performance needs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Vendors and Families
Major Vendors
AMD (Xilinx): Artix-7, Kintex-7, Virtex-7, Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+, Versal — broad range to heterogeneous platforms.
Intel (Altera): MAX 10, Cyclone V, Arria 10, Stratix 10, Agilex — from low-cost to high-performance datacenter parts.
Lattice Semiconductor: iCE40, MachXO, ECP — low-power, small form factors for edge devices.
Microchip (Microsemi): IGLOO, ProASIC, SmartFusion — radiation-tolerant and security-focused families.
Selection checklist
  • • Does the family include hard processors if you need SoC features?
  • • Are high-speed transceivers required for your interfaces?
  • • How many DSP blocks and block RAM are available for signal processing?
  • • What are the power and package constraints?
Concrete example
For a low-power IoT sensor node evaluate Lattice iCE40 or a small Artix device; for data-center acceleration evaluate Stratix or Agilex families.

screens.title: Hard IP and Heterogeneous Integration
screens.subtitle: Why vendors place processors, controllers, and accelerators on-die

narration.text: Modern FPGAs increasingly include hard intellectual property blocks—hard processors, DDR controllers, PCIe endpoints, and AI accelerators—directly in silicon. This hard IP changes the role of an FPGA from a pure reconfigurable fabric to a heterogeneous compute platform. The advantage is twofold: hard IP typically delivers better performance and energy efficiency than equivalent soft implementations in fabric, and it simplifies system integration by providing proven controllers. For example, embedding an ARM core enables a software-rich environment alongside reconfigurable logic, letting designers partition tasks between software and parallel hardware. However, this integration introduces new trade-offs: a device with heavy hard IP is less flexible in allocating silicon area for fabric logic, and families that emphasize hard cores are often more expensive. A common misconception is assuming every FPGA includes the same hard IP. In practice, families differ: some target embedded systems with Cortex-A processors, others are optimized for transceivers and DSP. Example: a Zynq-7000 part pairs ARM cores with fabric for mixed hardware-software systems, while Versal-class devices go further by adding AI inference engines. Takeaway: hard IP enables new classes of embedded systems but requires you to weigh integration benefits against flexibility and cost.

keyIdea.title: Hard IP trade-off
keyIdea.text: Embedding processors and controllers improves performance and integration but reduces fabric-only flexibility and can increase cost.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Hard IP and Heterogeneous Integration
Architecture

Hard blocks inside FPGA silicon

Embedding hard IP such as ARM cores, DDR controllers and PCIe endpoints brings software capabilities and high-performance engines onto the same die as the reconfigurable fabric, enabling heterogeneous systems.

• Better performance and power vs. soft implementations.
• Simplifies integration with standardized controllers.
• Reduces fabric area for pure logic when present.
• May increase device cost and change partitioning choices.
Concrete example
Zynq-7000 parts combine ARM cores with fabric for systems where software and parallel hardware share tasks. Versal-class devices add AI inference engines to accelerate machine learning workloads.
Misconception
Assuming all FPGAs offer the same hard IP. Check families for the exact controllers and cores included.
Key Takeaway

Hard IP turns FPGAs into heterogeneous platforms; choose families that match the system’s software and accelerator needs.

screens.title: High-Level Synthesis and Design Flow Changes
screens.subtitle: How HLS tools changed what designers synthesize into FPGAs

narration.text: High-Level Synthesis tools let designers describe algorithms in higher-level languages and have the tool generate hardware implementations. HLS changed the design flow by shifting some design effort from manual RTL coding to algorithmic specification and tuning. Where designers once hand-wrote register-transfer-level descriptions for each module, HLS enables compilation of C-like descriptions into pipelines and dataflow hardware. This is important because it broadens who can target FPGAs and accelerates development for complex compute kernels. A misconception is to assume HLS always produces optimal hardware; in many cases manual RTL still yields better area or performance. HLS is most effective when designers think in streaming and pipeline terms and validate resource constraints like available DSP blocks and on-chip memory. Concrete example: an FIR filter written in high-level code can be compiled by HLS into pipelined multiply-accumulate stages that map to DSP blocks, but the designer must still guide unrolling and latency trade-offs. Takeaway: HLS raises abstraction and speeds development, but understanding fabric primitives and resource budgets remains critical to produce efficient FPGA implementations. High-Level Synthesis and Design Flow Changes means hls raises abstraction and productivity but requires guidance to meet area and performance targets; manual rtl still matters for tight optimizations.. In practical terms, how hls tools changed what designers synthesize into fpgas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: HLS trade-off
keyIdea.text: HLS raises abstraction and productivity but requires guidance to meet area and performance targets; manual RTL still matters for tight optimizations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › High-Level Synthesis and Design Flow Changes
Concept

HLS shifts abstraction upward

HLS compiles higher-level algorithmic descriptions into hardware implementations, enabling faster development of compute kernels that use DSPs and block RAMs.

Example flow
  1. 1. Describe the algorithm in a C-like style, emphasizing streaming and loops.
  2. 2. Apply pragmas to direct unrolling, pipelining, and resource mapping.
  3. 3. Compile with HLS to generate RTL and map to DSP and memory blocks.
Concrete example

An FIR filter described in high-level code can be compiled into pipelined multiply-accumulate stages that map to DSP blocks and block RAM buffers.

Misconception
HLS makes hardware optimal automatically. In reality, HLS needs designer guidance to meet tight area or timing goals.
Key Takeaway

Use HLS to raise productivity for algorithmic kernels, but keep fabric resource budgets and manual optimizations in mind for best results.

screens.title: Moore's Law and Density: Enabling Hard IP
screens.subtitle: How transistor scaling allowed integration of processors and accelerators

narration.text: Moore’s Law—transistor density roughly doubling over time—enabled vendors to allocate silicon area to specialized hard IP blocks inside FPGAs. As transistor budgets grew, designers could include block R A M, multipliers, and entire processor cores without sacrificing fabric capacity. This shift meant that chips could combine software-capable processors with reconfigurable logic on a single die, saving board area and improving latency between software and hardware. The practical result is today’s heterogeneous platforms where a fabric accelerates hotspots called from an embedded processor. A misconception is thinking Moore’s Law alone guarantees better performance per dollar; integration choices and packaging also matter. For designers, the important insight is that dense processes allow more on-die specialization: vendors can add DDR controllers, PCIe, and AI engines because they have the transistor budget to do so. Example: Versal-class devices include AI inference engines and hard interconnect to support data-center acceleration. Takeaway: transistor scaling made it feasible to trade some reconfigurable area for specialized blocks that improve system-level performance and reduce development complexity. keyIdea.text: As transistor counts rose, vendors could integrate hard processors and accelerators, turning FPGAs into heterogeneous compute platforms.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Moore's Law and Density: Enabling Hard IP
Claim

Density allowed specialization

As processes scaled, vendors could dedicate silicon to hard IP blocks such as processors, DDR controllers and AI engines while still offering abundant fabric for custom logic.

• More transistors let vendors mix fabric with hard, optimized IP.
• Integration reduces board-level complexity and latency between CPU and logic.
• Packaging and economics still influence how much hard IP appears on a family.
Practical example
A Versal-class device packs AI inference engines and high-speed interconnect that would have been impossible on early processes. The result is higher system throughput for targeted workloads.
Misconception
Do not assume every newer node is optimal for your design. Power, IO, and package choices still matter more than raw transistor counts in some embedded use cases.
Key Takeaway

Transistor scaling enabled vendors to add hard IP that improves system-level performance, but designers must balance integration against flexibility and cost.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from the chapter

narration.text: These are the three core concepts to carry forward. First, the programmable-logic lineage: PROMs demonstrated LUT-based logic, PALs improved efficiency by sharing product terms, CPLDs introduced electrically erasable interconnect, and FPGAs provided a routed array of small logic blocks. Second, Ross Freeman’s FPGA insight: a two-dimensional array of logic blocks plus programmable routing enabled scalable reconfigurable hardware and spatial parallelism. Third, generational trends and vendor specializations: embedded R A M, DSP, hard processors, and AI accelerators appear over successive generations, and different vendors and families emphasize low power, security, throughput, or heterogeneous integration. Keep these distinctions in mind when reading datasheets or choosing a device for an embedded project. keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Lineage, Freeman’s routing insight, and generational trends are the pillars for understanding modern FPGA architecture choices.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Key Concepts
Lineage
PROM → PAL → CPLD → FPGA: each step improved efficiency, reprogrammability or routing flexibility.
FPGA Insight
Ross Freeman’s array plus routing model enabled scalable, general-purpose reconfigurable hardware.
Generations
From LUTs to embedded memory, DSP, hard processors and AI accelerators—vendors added capabilities across generations.
Summary Takeaway

Know the lineage, the FPGA routing insight, and how generations map to capabilities. Those three guide effective device selection and architecture trade-offs.

narration.text: Keep these concise reminders when you design or evaluate embedded FPGA systems. First: PROMs are LUTs and scale poorly for many inputs. Second: PALs and CPLDs provided efficient, reprogrammable glue logic; CPLDs added non-volatile configuration. Third: the FPGA’s routed array unlocked scalable parallelism; generations afterward added on-die memory, DSP, hard processors, and AI engines. When you read datasheets, prioritize the metrics relevant to your system: logic capacity, block R A M, DSP count, presence of hard processors, and transceivers. Finally, match vendor families to application needs—low-power edge, security-focused, or high-throughput data center acceleration. These brief points will help you decide which family to evaluate next for your embedded project. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What to Remember
LUT scaling
PROMs require 2^n storage and don’t scale for wide inputs.
Reprogrammability
CPLDs offered EEPROM-based reprogramming; FPGAs used volatile config but provided flexibility and scale.
Resource checklist
When comparing parts check logic cells, block RAM, DSPs, hard IP, and transceiver availability.
Final prompt

Which vendor family will you investigate first for your next embedded design, and which metrics will guide your choice?
